CaseNumber: 00846618

case_summary.summary: Multiple lost secondary console alerts appeared on GRS10 units in the 5th floor Mother Baby unit, even though none of the consoles were actually offline. Investigation found the RCB3 NUC was configured to monitor itself but would not accept a heartbeat from itself; clearing this condition from the database (no reboot needed) resolved the alert, although the same type of issue had occurred before.
case_summary.reported_issue: Multiple lost secondary console alerts were displayed on GRS10 units in the 5th floor Mother Baby unit.
case_summary.product: Nurse Call - GRS10 / RCB3 NUC
case_summary.actions_taken: Logged into the ADV server and ran a lost secondary query
Confirmed none of the 5th floor Mother Baby GRS10 units were actually offline
Rebooted the NUC (alerts cleared temporarily but returned)
Rebooted all GRS10 units in Mother Baby, which did not clear the alerts
Cleared the self-monitoring condition from the database
case_summary.resolution: RCB3 NUC was set to monitor itself, but would not accept heartbeat from itself. This had to be cleared from the database. No reboot was needed after this was done to clear the alert.
case_summary.status: resolved
case_summary.key_points: Root cause: RCB3 NUC configured to monitor itself and failing to accept its own heartbeat
Same type of issue had occurred before; flagged as no further action required
Rebooting the NUC and GRS10 units did not permanently clear the alert; clearing from the database did

comment_summary: A nursing unit repeatedly raised a Lost Secondary Console call that returned after the call was cancelled and the NUC rebooted. Reviewing the basesystemsettings folder showed every secondary console in the NUC's secondary list was heartbeating except the NUC's own route id, rcb3-037221Y2WM2, which was itself present in that list; the NUC was not heartbeating with itself on either the ethernet or loopback interface, and it was the only device in the hospital with its own route id in its secondary list. The cause was identified as a monitoring criteria for a single room pointing at itself, so the NUC expected connections and heartbeats from itself and raised a Lost Secondary call when they never arrived. The fix was validated on a restored copy of the customer database before deleting the self-referencing monitoring criteria at the site and pushing configuration, after which the lost secondary call cleared with no device reboot, and no new lost secondary calls appeared for a week.

root_cause_summary: Updated configuration to resolve
investigation_details: There was a lost secondary console call that could not be cleared by any procedures to clear stuck calls - like marking the call as cancelled in the database and bouncing device service / devices.   I examined the secondary console list for the NUC that was placing the call.   This was RB 5 MB RCB3 NUC (RCB3) - 10.155.66.0 - rcb3-037221Y2WM2.  The nuc’s own ip address appeared in the list, and this was unique for the whole site - no other device had a reference to itself as a secondary.   Looking to see where the list was coming from, I found table function dbo.SecondaryConsoleConfig_GetByOrgUnitId_45.  By running the sql contained in the function, I determined that the reference to itself was coming from a monitoring criteria consisting of only a single room, many call types, and 1 org unit.    This monitoring criteria was somehow orphaned (not deleted or left behind somehow.)   After testing for safety on my machine, I deleted the monitoring criteria with sql statements, pushed configuration, and the lost secondary call disappeared.
troubleshooting_steps: Confirmed correct sw on both RCB and GRS10H. 

Confirmed no call forwarding set for the GRS10H. 

Confirmed no additional monitored units for GRS10H. 

Checked syslogs. No errors for either device. Checked configuration service log. 

Did see some other devices in the syslogs showing the invalid URI lines. 

Confirmed both effected devices are checking in successfully. 

Ran netstat on both devices. Confirmed they successfully establish to each other. 

Performed global push. No change. Purged configuration. No change. 

Forced push sw to both. No change.
troubleshooting_results: The alert makes no sense since the RCB NUC itself is not showing lost. Also the netstat proves the nuc and GRS10h are connected.
verification_summary: Determined the reference to itself was coming from a monitoring criteria consisting of only a single room, many call types, and 1 org unit. Pushed configuration, and the Lost Secondary Console alert cleared. Proper operation was confirmed & there were no patient safety issues reported. Although updating the configuration resolved issue; unable to determine how issue was caused.
rca_review_comments: Unknown how the NUC got into this state but issue has been resolved.

summary: Unable to Clear Lost RCB without resetting NUC
description: Whenever they have to reboot an RCB3 (either due to troubleshooting or moving it from staging, etc.) there is a Lost RCB alert that is placed that stays on the system despite the RCB3 and GRS5 coming up properly (GRS5 displays a Primary Console Down message while in this state).  They have found that clearing the config and rebooting the NUC clears the alert as the RCB/GRS5 are online just fine.  We found that resetting the dhcp service on the NUC (via the command _sudo udhcpc renew_) clears the alerts as well.  Further strange behavior exists with the system as the end devices can ping the NUC, however the NUC was not able to ping any of the devices, but only the device that is rebooted is being reported as lost.  The NUC has been replaced as has the cable to rule them out.  This can be re-produced by simply rebooting any RCB3 on the 1st FL ED Unit.  All devices are on the correct firmware - 3.9.101.8.
comment_summary: A site could not clear a Lost RCB alert without resetting the NUC. Investigation reproduced the condition on site and found that after an RCB reboot the old socket on port 50005 was never released, so connections stacked up on the NUC until it was rebooted, though this was judged a symptom rather than the cause. Deeper testing showed that after an RCB reboot, ping worked but SSH and connectivity between the NUC and the RCB failed for 8 to 18 minutes before self-clearing, and packet captures taken with tcpdump on both devices showed an ARP duplicate-use warning for the NUC address 172.20.95.249 from an unknown MAC 54:75:d0:26:df:cc that was not present in the deviceconnection tables, plus duplicated hops in a traceroute from the RCB to the NUC while in the bad state. The customer found a NAT configuration on a Cisco device that was producing the duplicate IP behavior; after it was removed, rebooted RCBs reconnected automatically and the alerts cleared.

summary: NC - Basement PBX - Lost Unit Server
description: Customer details:

Acct # 605080

Acct name:Lubbock County Hospital District



Issue- PBX console (Secondary GRS10) was showing 30 lost unit server alerts. Unable to receive Code blue alerts. Checking performance of the GRS10 it remains at a constant 98/99% for CPU usage for NNC. 

Cause- The CPU usage is due to the GRS10 failing to make connections to other NNC devices over port 50005. Most of the connections show a TIME_WAIT instead of ESTABLISHED. Further probing revealed these connection failures was due to a disabled GRS10H NUC on the same subnet as our effected GRS10. 

Resolution: Rebooting the disabled GRS10H NUC resolved the issue of the failed connections on our effected GRS10. After the reboot connections were established and NNC CPU utilization on the GRS10 went down. 

Reason for RCA- We need to confirm why a disabled NUC would cause this sort of issue.
comment_summary: A basement PBX console reported Lost Unit Server alerts, together with high NNC CPU utilization on a GRS10 even though the bed plugins were not in use. Removing all plugins except calls and repeatedly rebooting the GRS10H NUC cut the alerts from 30 to 17 and finally cleared them, although the plugin-related spiking was supposed to have been resolved after 3.9.401. Later work found Lost Unit Server and lost secondary console alerts persisting for a nursing unit that was disabled in ECT, and the alerts cleared only after removing that disabled unit from the secondary unit monitoring of the other primary console and of the PBX. In the final session, re-enabling monitoring and rebooting the PBX no longer reproduced the alerts, and the engineer disabled SNTP on a POE switch (firmware 1.0.23) that had been rebooted, then left the site monitoring for recurrence.

comment_summary: The defect is that cancelled lost service alerts continue to display on the staff console when GRS10h staff consoles and RCB3s are configured as a NUC. Investigation concluded only GRS10h and RCB3 acting as NUCs are affected, so the title and description were updated; if GRS10 or RCB/RCB2 NUC units showed the same behavior the cause would likely be different. The initial theory was an order inversion of the source and destination URIs in the header of the alert socket on port 50005, with no corresponding change on legacy devices. Reproduction steps exist only for GRS10h, which made writing a verification test for RCB3 difficult, and a large set of direct and regression tests ultimately passed across PDP26, PDP28, PDR0 and PDR1.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
The duplo app needed to invert the source and destination in the alert socket message header.  The order being inverted caused some messages to not get properly routed to the nuc (if the nuc was a grs10h or rcb3) from the server.  This also caused some adjustments in the legacy client because the changed caused some connection and routing issues for the legacy devices for secondary or capture scenarios( true for both duplo nuc -> legacy monitoring or legacy nuc -> duplo monitoring).  The legacy devices now more directly associate (direct callback) received data on the alert socket to the object modeling that device.  Instead of just associating the two objects via URIs.  
Impact Assessment:  
NNC - Call Placement and Handling - Minor - Secondary and Capture connections should be a focus to make sure that connections are maintained and that alerts flow as expected.  
Platform Impact:  
grs5/grs7, rcb/rcb2/rcb3, grs10/grs10h  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  24/SEPT/2025  
Attendees - Eric Davis (Quality Engineering), Stephen Moore (Development Engineering)  
Minutes - This code change is around how alert packets are routed and affects both duplo and legacy devices. No testing around UI, VOIP, locating, dome lights or annuciation need to be included in the regression test list. In the regression meeting, we did identify some areas missing from the regression filter like reminders, service start/stop and capture/swing tests. Tests to cover these areas were added and agreed upon by both QE and Development.   
No additional software components need verification for this code change.

description: Background: University of Miami is currently undergoing a hardware installation, where they are replacing older hardware (RCB1s and 2s, GRS5s, and GRS10s) with new hardware (RCB3s, GRS7s, GRS10Hs).  
  
Issue: On **Thursday, June 1st**, it was pointed out to on-site teams that the PBX console (which also served as the PBX NUC) was bouncing a Lost Unit Srv alert. The PBX is there to monitor for Code Calls and nothing else, making this a potential safety issue.  
This was reported to the IE behind the project, **Mark Peterson**. He proceeded to replace the GRS10, thinking it may have been something with the console. When this failed to provide the desired outcome, he set up an RCB3 to act as a NUC for the PBX to alleviate stress on the console. This also did not work. He then contacted Tech Support for assistance.

Troubleshooting/Investigation: At first, it was discovered that the GRS10’s message queue was being overloaded with messages from devices across the network. This was confirmed when I cleared the Secondary Nursing Unit list and the alerts stopped bouncing. I then proceeded to add floors back to the SNU list until the issue was recreated. The limit at the moment was five. Adding a sixth produced the bouncing alert, and adding a seventh floor put the GRS10 into a reboot cycle. These were alleviated, again, by clearing the SNU list and building it back up to five.

With the assistance of **Stephen Moore**, we were able to determine the sockets being used by the PBX were being closed. He identified that the PBX was sending out the initial handshake, which was being acknowledged by target devices. However, the sockets were being closed almost immediately thereafter.

We worked with the site’s IT team to verify the network was working as expected. DHCP and DNS are in working order, there are no firewalls in place to disrupt traffic. investigation_details: There was a lost secondary console call that could not be cleared by any procedures to clear stuck calls - like marking the call as cancelled in the database and bouncing device service / devices.   I examined the secondary console list for the NUC that was placing the call.   This was RB 5 MB RCB3 NUC (RCB3) - 10.155.66.0 - rcb3-037221Y2WM2.  The nuc’s own ip address appeared in the list, and this was unique for the whole site - no other device had a reference to itself as a secondary.   Looking to see where the list was coming from, I found table function dbo.SecondaryConsoleConfig_GetByOrgUnitId_45.  By running the sql contained in the function, I determined that the reference to itself was coming from a monitoring criteria consisting of only a single room, many call types, and 1 org unit.    This monitoring criteria was somehow orphaned (not deleted or left behind somehow.)   After testing for safety on my machine, I deleted the monitoring criteria with sql statements, pushed configuration, and the lost secondary call disappeared.

Confirmed no call forwarding set for the GRS10H. 

Confirmed no additional monitored units for GRS10H. 

Checked syslogs. No errors for either device. Checked configuration service log. 

Did see some other devices in the syslogs showing the invalid URI lines. 

Confirmed both effected devices are checking in successfully. 

Ran netstat on both devices. Confirmed they successfully establish to each other. 

Performed global push. No change. Purged configuration. No change. 

Forced push sw to both. No change.
troubleshooting_results: The alert makes no sense since the RCB NUC itself is not showing lost. Also the netstat proves the nuc and GRS10h are connected.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
The duplo app needed to invert the source and destination in the alert socket message header.  The order being inverted caused some messages to not get properly routed to the nuc (if the nuc was a grs10h or rcb3) from the server.  This also caused some adjustments in the legacy client because the changed caused some connection and routing issues for the legacy devices for secondary or capture scenarios( true for both duplo nuc -> legacy monitoring or legacy nuc -> duplo monitoring).  The legacy devices now more directly associate (direct callback) received data on the alert socket to the object modeling that device.  Instead of just associating the two objects via URIs.  
Impact Assessment:  
NNC - Call Placement and Handling - Minor - Secondary and Capture connections should be a focus to make sure that connections are maintained and that alerts flow as expected.  
Platform Impact:  
grs5/grs7, rcb/rcb2/rcb3, grs10/grs10h  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  24/SEPT/2025  
Attendees - Eric Davis (Quality Engineering), Stephen Moore (Development Engineering)  
Minutes - This code change is around how alert packets are routed and affects both duplo and legacy devices. No testing around UI, VOIP, locating, dome lights or annuciation need to be included in the regression test list. In the regression meeting, we did identify some areas missing from the regression filter like reminders, service start/stop and capture/swing tests. Tests to cover these areas were added and agreed upon by both QE and Development.   
No additional software components need verification for this code change.

summary: Investigate 6 returned RCB3s from Conroe Medical Center, Conroe Texas
description: Four of the 6, have damaged capacitors. C13_POE was missing on 3 of the boards and C1B was missing or damaged on 2 of the boards.  2 boards have no visible damage.  One Equipment Jack was returned where the studs that are welded to the back of the plate were broken off.
root_cause_summary: The investigation determined that the primary failure was a manufacturing process error at the contract manufacturer. Analysis of the returned RCB3 units identified one device (SN: 4618 30B WIS) that had failed Final Configuration Testing (FCT), specifically the Dome Light Speaker test, yet was still shipped to the customer. Further investigation confirmed that the device's VPD EEPROM had not been properly programmed and the manufacturer verified that the unit was released despite a failed FCT result due to operator error.

Of the six returned units, four exhibited obvious physical damage, including missing or damaged C13_POE and C1B capacitors, which prevented normal operation and suggested handling or installation-related damage. A second unit (SN: 4718 04E WIS) was fully functional during testing and no product defect could be identified.

The contract manufacturer subsequently confirmed that the failed unit was mistakenly shipped despite not passing production testing and committed to retraining the operator responsible for the test station.
investigation_details: Investigated 2 out of the 6 units (4 units were damaged and could not be powered on). No issue was detected on the RCB3 SN: 4718 04E WIS. The unit with SN: 4618 30B WIS was found to have failed the FCT.
rca_review_comments: The confirmed product failure was caused by a manufacturing quality-control breakdown in which an RCB3 that failed Final Configuration Testing was inadvertently shipped to the customer. Investigation found the device had not completed manufacturing configuration successfully and lacked proper VPD programming. The contract manufacturer verified that the release occurred due to operator error at the FCT station and implemented corrective action through operator retraining. Additional returned units exhibited physical component damage consistent with handling or installation-related causes rather than a systemic product defect.

root_cause_summary: The investigation determined that the primary failure was a manufacturing process error at the contract manufacturer. Analysis of the returned RCB3 units identified one device (SN: 4618 30B WIS) that had failed Final Configuration Testing (FCT), specifically the Dome Light Speaker test, yet was still shipped to the customer. Further investigation confirmed that the device's VPD EEPROM had not been properly programmed and the manufacturer verified that the unit was released despite a failed FCT result due to operator error.

Of the six returned units, four exhibited obvious physical damage, including missing or damaged C13_POE and C1B capacitors, which prevented normal operation and suggested handling or installation-related damage. A second unit (SN: 4718 04E WIS) was fully functional during testing and no product defect could be identified.

The contract manufacturer subsequently confirmed that the failed unit was mistakenly shipped despite not passing production testing and committed to retraining the operator responsible for the test station.
investigation_details: Investigated 2 out of the 6 units (4 units were damaged and could not be powered on). No issue was detected on the RCB3 SN: 4718 04E WIS. The unit with SN: 4618 30B WIS was found to have failed the FCT.
rca_review_comments: The confirmed product failure was caused by a manufacturing quality-control breakdown in which an RCB3 that failed Final Configuration Testing was inadvertently shipped to the customer. Investigation found the device had not completed manufacturing configuration successfully and lacked proper VPD programming. The contract manufacturer verified that the release occurred due to operator error at the FCT station and implemented corrective action through operator retraining. Additional returned units exhibited physical component damage consistent with handling or installation-related causes rather than a systemic product defect.

summary: Calls not clearing from Status board (intermittent)
description: VNC 4.1

After the upgrade site is experiencing intermittent stuck calls on status board, These calls are not showing on end devices, GRS5,GRS7 or GRS10’s only Status board

Most of the stuck calls are Bed exit and chair alarm calls

However I have seen a call cord disconnect be stuck, we went to the room, placed another call cord disconnect call, plugged call cord in, the newest call cleared but the old did not, which it remained on status board.

Tried multiple tests around 12:30 pm local, 3:30 est, North tower 4th floor RM 71. we placed bed exit calls, entered the room. adjusted the bed and canceled from the GRS7, alert then cleared from Status board.

While cleaning up the test room, customer turned bed exit off. Took weights off bed, zeroed the bed, call triggered and remained active in status board but not on the GRS10. Had to restart services to clear.

Restarting status board services clears the calls every time

This issue seemingly is happening across the whole site, North tower 4th floor showing the most issues.
comment_summary: Calls intermittently failed to clear from the Status board at sites running 4.1.200, severely enough that one customer paused remaining upgrade projects. Device Service Host logs for a stuck call showed the de-duplication logic failing to trigger, producing a SQL error 2601 "Cannot insert duplicate key row in object 'NCC.V_ActiveCall' with unique index 'AK_UniqueActiveCallGUID'" so call creation was abandoned, after which every subsequent status update (Answered, Cancel) failed with SQL error 257 "Implicit conversion from data type nvarchar to timestamp is not allowed" and the call never cleared. The suspicion was that a secondary or monitoring console reports the alert with the same BaseCallID but a different RequestingDeviceId, causing IsDuplicateAlertNotification() in AlertMessageHandler.cs to fail, and the affected units all used secondary consoles and unit monitoring. A separate bug was also found in the call_update stored procedure, where the row edition check compares @RowEdition to itself rather than to the stored RowEdition. The workaround that resolved it was setting MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads to 1 in the Device Service appsettings.json file, after which no further stuck-call reports were made at either site.

root_cause_summary: Recent moves to multi-threaded processing in the Device service introduced a race condition where a secondary notification from a console monitoring the location was treated as a new call rather than a duplicate.  This caused an issue where it would inject a secondary copy of the call into the RabbitMQ bus, which caused it to appear as a duplicate while the call is still active, and a stuck call when the active call is cancelled.

comment_summary: Several sites showed no SDC activity. The RabbitMQ nodes were healthy, but Mirth had stopped processing messages for six customers since around 7:16 that morning, while continuing to receive and queue their messages and processing normally for all other customers. An earlier, similar incident caused by Mirth's SQL databases filling up was ruled out because the database was healthy and that incident had affected every customer rather than a subset. Restarting the channels for the six affected customers restored processing within minutes, leaving a backlog to work through, and the thread concludes that the most likely cause is a race condition in the processing threads on the Mirth server, with no way to confirm it after the fact.

root_cause_summary: The root cause of this issue is unknown. The most likely cause is a race condition with the processing threads on the Mirth server that ended up freezing up the impacted customers channels. Other potential causes have been eliminated. The CPU/RAM and Memory on the Mirth server look healthy at the time of the incident and not every customer was impacted, which eliminates most issues with the Mirth VM itself. Another thought was a potential database issue, but restarting the channels resolved the issue with no further action taken to clear up database space, which makes that unlikely. If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause.
investigation_details: RabbitMQ nodes looked healthy and all up and functional, along with the federations. Next we looked to Mirth, where I found that a number of customers (six total, including the three in the RCA) were beginning to queue up. In the channels for these customers, I found that they were up and actively receiving and queueing messages, but were not processing anything new. The last processed message in any of these customers channels was about the same time (7:16am). 

To try and resolve this, I restarted the ADT channels for these customers. After they came up again, they all began processing messages again. While messages had queued up for a few hours (we resolved this issue around 9:30am), most customers had cleared and were caught up to normal again by the early afternoon.
verification_summary: Root cause inconclusive. After restarting ADT, messages started to process. Further investigation would be needed if issue were to recur.
rca_review_comments: If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause. We have monitored Mirth the past week since the incident and this has not happened again.

summary: Race Condition with Call creation from monitored units
description: https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1625   
  
When units are being monitored, the system will report multiple of the same call (GUID/BaseCallID) to the Device Service, one from the NUC of the unit where the call was generated, and N number of calls from the Consoles that are monitoring the NUC.  The system will add the call to the SQL database and then onto an in-memory list.  The system will look on the in-memory list to determine if a call that has been reported has already been raised.  Occasionally the 2nd notification of the call will come in before the injection into SQL and adding onto the in-memory list has finished occurring.  This race condition will cause the system to incorrectly identify the monitoring console’s report as a new call.  This will fail to process and eventually result in a call that is stuck in both the database and StatusBoard (RabbitMQ specifically).  
  
In the customer environment, they have a separate SQL server and other external factors that could contribute to this race condition occurring that would have to be emulated for testing.
comment_summary: The defect concerns a race condition in call creation from monitored units. Development stated the potential race condition has existed since 2012, with no explanation yet for why it only appeared with 4.1.200 and why not all 4.1.200 sites see it, and noted the same change must also be made in the cc-nc-lib-alertComponent repository. A SQL loop repeatedly selecting from dbo.call with a half second delay was used to put load on the system while attempting reproduction. The defect could not be reproduced on PDR0 and the direct test P1575-TEST-3707 passed there after being blocked in PDP28.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
Moving the default value from 2 to 1 for the MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads in the appsettings.json and code causes the service to only process 1 message at a time.  This allows the system to avoid the race condition while minimizing code changes/regression.  
Before: Failure to process a SQL Insert before a monitored NUC reports a call results in calls incorrectly being identified as a new call instead of a duplicate, throwing errors in the DeviceService log and having the calls stuck in the DB & on StatusBoard.  
After: Device Service correctly identifies the calls as duplicates.  
Impact Assessment:  
NCP - Error Handling and System Alerting - Trivial  
Platform Impact:  
N/A  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  27/OCT/2025  
Attendees - Josh Watkins (Development Engineering), Kate Papalava (Quality Engineering)  
Minutes - The call processing logic is not impacted by the change, so the direct test is sufficient for verification.  
Additional Software Components:  
N/A
steps_taken: 1\. Configure a console to monitor another unit for Normal Calls.  
2\. Set up a method to prevent the SQL call completing before the 2nd notification comes in.  
3\. Place a normal call from a monitored location.
actual_results: The system treats the 2nd notification as a new call, causing SQL errors in the Device Service log and the call is stuck in the database and in Statusboard.
expected_results: The system should detect that the 2nd notification is a duplicate and not re-process the call.
work_around: Restarting RabbitMQ service

summary: Status Board periodically fails to update bed data/calls
description: Site was experiencing no updates to statusboard on either Chrome or IE. Press F5 on browser and status board would update, but continue to be stale from the point of refresh. Found Rabbit not processing any messages, but running. Restarted Bridge and Rabbit as described and Rabbit began to process messages. There have been several RabbitMQ crashes over time, so I suspect it will crash again and create the same stale status board issue. Currently monitoring.
comment_summary: Status Board periodically failed to update bed data and calls, recovering only when refreshed, at multiple sites. Bed exit calls were confirmed to reach the database with no bridge service errors, and browser observation showed messages travelling from the Service Fabric service to the web client but the client never acknowledging them, with messages stopping once SignalR reported its error; only the Service Fabric logs contained errors, not the advanced service or Windows event logs. After RabbitMQ, Service Fabric and the advanced services were restarted, bed, locating and call data again reached the web client and the database, but a remaining problem appeared in the SignalR communication between the Status Board API service and the web client, where the client fails to acknowledge messages so the connection works for about two minutes before SignalR closes or resets it. A similar occurrence was reported at another site on an earlier version, and the service cloud case was closed with the resolution recorded as restarting RabbitMQ and the bridge service and confirming calls displayed as expected.

However I have seen a call cord disconnect be stuck, we went to the room, placed another call cord disconnect call, plugged call cord in, the newest call cleared but the old did not, which it remained on status board.

Tried multiple tests around 12:30 pm local, 3:30 est, North tower 4th floor RM 71. we placed bed exit calls, entered the room. adjusted the bed and canceled from the GRS7, alert then cleared from Status board.

comment_summary: Calls intermittently failed to clear from the Status board at sites running 4.1.200, severely enough that one customer paused remaining upgrade projects. Device Service Host logs for a stuck call showed the de-duplication logic failing to trigger, producing a SQL error 2601 "Cannot insert duplicate key row in object 'NCC.V_ActiveCall' with unique index 'AK_UniqueActiveCallGUID'" so call creation was abandoned, after which every subsequent status update (Answered, Cancel) failed with SQL error 257 "Implicit conversion from data type nvarchar to timestamp is not allowed" and the call never cleared. The suspicion was that a secondary or monitoring console reports the alert with the same BaseCallID but a different RequestingDeviceId, causing IsDuplicateAlertNotification() in AlertMessageHandler.cs to fail, and the affected units all used secondary consoles and unit monitoring. A separate bug was also found in the call_update stored procedure, where the row edition check compares @RowEdition to itself rather than to the stored RowEdition. The workaround that resolved it was setting MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads to 1 in the Device Service appsettings.json file, after which no further stuck-call reports were made at either site.

root_cause_summary: The root cause of this issue is unknown. The most likely cause is a race condition with the processing threads on the Mirth server that ended up freezing up the impacted customers channels. Other potential causes have been eliminated. The CPU/RAM and Memory on the Mirth server look healthy at the time of the incident and not every customer was impacted, which eliminates most issues with the Mirth VM itself. Another thought was a potential database issue, but restarting the channels resolved the issue with no further action taken to clear up database space, which makes that unlikely. If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause.
investigation_details: RabbitMQ nodes looked healthy and all up and functional, along with the federations. Next we looked to Mirth, where I found that a number of customers (six total, including the three in the RCA) were beginning to queue up. In the channels for these customers, I found that they were up and actively receiving and queueing messages, but were not processing anything new. The last processed message in any of these customers channels was about the same time (7:16am). 

To try and resolve this, I restarted the ADT channels for these customers. After they came up again, they all began processing messages again. While messages had queued up for a few hours (we resolved this issue around 9:30am), most customers had cleared and were caught up to normal again by the early afternoon.
verification_summary: Root cause inconclusive. After restarting ADT, messages started to process. Further investigation would be needed if issue were to recur.

investigation_details: ````
The customer reported one patient (Same MRN ) appearing in two rooms simultaneously in Voalte Admin Client at UPMC Pinnacle West Shore (NC 4.1.200): PatientID `337242` in Room 549 (LocationID `2185`) and PatientID `337243` in Room 547 (LocationID `2246`). Manual discharge from Voalte Admin Client failed with the generic toast "Your action could not be completed." HL7 ADT messages from the customer's EMR for this patient were also being silently rejected.
We pulled the customer's `AdvancedServiceLogs - UPMC Westshore.zip` archive (110 MB) and traced the failure end-to-end:
1. **Code path traced.** `PatientStaffServiceHost`'s admit pipeline (`PatientADTController.ProcessCoreADTAction` → `PatientADTService.ProcessAdmitAction` → `PatientAggregationService.CreatePatientAndAssignLocation`) validates MRN uniqueness via `PatientDAL.cs:88` (Insert) and `:231` (Update). The check calls `Patient.IsUniqueMrn` (`Patient.cs:557`) which executes a separate scalar `SELECT dbo.Patient_UniqueMRN(@MRN, @PatientId)` — independent of the subsequent `Patient_Insert_55` / `Patient_Update_55` stored proc.
